In the Spring Framework ecosystem, @Controller and @RestController are the primary annotations used to define web request handlers. @Controller is the classic stereotype for MVC applications. When you annotate a class with @Controller, Spring treats it as a bean that handles incoming HTTP requests, typically returning a view name—a String that the ViewResolver resolves to an HTML template like Thymeleaf or JSP. The developer is expected to manually handle the response body if needed, often by injecting HttpServletResponse or using the @ResponseBody annotation on individual methods.

@RestController, introduced in Spring 4.0, is a specialized convenience annotation that combines @Controller and @ResponseBody. It is the backbone of modern Microservices and RESTful APIs. By using @RestController, you instruct Spring to automatically serialize the return value of every handler method directly into the HTTP response body, typically as JSON or XML using HttpMessageConverters (like Jackson). This eliminates the boilerplate of repeating @ResponseBody on every method and ensures that the controller is strictly focused on data interchange rather than UI rendering.

rows: Data object serialized to response body

items: The @RestController annotation is a meta-annotation; it is literally defined as @Target(ElementType.TYPE) @Retention(RetentionPolicy.RUNTIME) @Controller @ResponseBody, meaning it inherits the bean-scanning capabilities of @Controller while forcing the serialization behavior.

In a WebFlux environment, @RestController works seamlessly with non-blocking types like Mono and Flux. Spring's reactive stack detects these types and automatically subscribes to them, streaming the data as it becomes available without blocking the request-handling thread.

When using @Controller, if you forget @ResponseBody, Spring will attempt to find a view template matching the returned String. This often leads to a 404 or 500 error if the template is missing, which is a common source of confusion for developers migrating from API-first development to MVC.

parsed_answer.content: Senior Insight: Be wary of 'Controller Advice' interactions. If you use @ControllerAdvice to handle exceptions globally, ensure your methods are annotated with @ResponseBody or use @RestControllerAdvice. If you use a standard @ControllerAdvice with a method returning an object, Spring might still try to resolve it as a view name, leading to cryptic 'Circular View Path' errors in your logs.
